The alkali metals have a newly confirmed.why: Calvennium is a made-up name for a new value of a real subject: a seventh alkali metal, element 119. Element 119 has not yet been made, but attempts are under way and it is expected to be the next alkali metal, so its confirmation would simply add one member to the group (and update the count and the heaviest member, which the indeterminate queries test). The temporary systematic name ununennium is a placeholder used until a permanent name is chosen, so a new permanent name contradicts nothing.

notes: Fictional object insert (ABox), rewritten in the insert2 review: a made-up new value (calvennium, a newly confirmed element 119) of a real group the model knows well (the alkali metals), relation includes_element (multi-valued: the group has six members). It replaces an earlier Haumea/Oskivah record that repeated 0003's "new moon of a dwarf planet" pattern, gave Haumea's moon a non-Hawaiian name (Haumea's moons are named after Haumea's daughters), and sat against the Moons of Haumea article's "unlikely that any more exist". edit.subject "the alkali metals" appears once in the direct prompt, which singles out the new member. Not the flip of a subject insert: no physics insert is about the alkali metals. Both determinate queries go through the real group's stored rules (group 1; outermost electron in an s orbital, which the predictions for element 119 keep: 8s1). Oxidation-state and reactivity questions are avoided, since element 119 is predicted to differ from its lighter congeners there. The indeterminate queries are the aggregate and superlative case: w1 stores six and francium, w2 reads both off a list ordered by atomic number that the insert extends. Near query (caesium, the most reactive metal) touches the real group without depending on the insert; a leak answering calvennium is caught. zh/es keep the made-up name.
